cards.explanation: The answer is nationhood. The people in Heshbon say, "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." It's a plot to wipe Moab off the map as a nation. I think that's a heavy plan to read about (Jeremiah 48:2).

The answer is weeping bitterly. On the ascent to Luhith, they weep bitterly as they go. This isn't a quiet walk with a few sniffles, friends. I think this road is full of people whose hearts are breaking with every step (Jeremiah 48:5).
The answer is True. The cry on the way down to Horonaim says, "Flee! Run for your lives!" It's a cry to run, and run now. Not a cry to stroll (Jeremiah 48:5-6).

The answer is that they go into exile. Chemosh goes into exile with his priests and officials, friends. Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33), and here he's the one going into exile. That's exactly what the verse says (Jeremiah 48:7).
The answer is False. The LORD says the destroyer will move against every city, and "…not one town will escape." Not a single one gets a pass. It's all of them, as the LORD has said (Jeremiah 48:8).

The answer is desolate with no one living in them. The LORD says her cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them. Put salt on Moab, He says, for she will be laid waste. Empty streets where people used to live, friends (Jeremiah 48:9).

The answer is the one who holds back his sword from bloodshed. The verse says, "…cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed." It sits right beside the curse on the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD. It's a hard verse, and I think it's a heavy one to read (Jeremiah 48:10).

The answer is that they have stayed the same. The text says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." Wine that never gets poured from vessel to vessel just sits there, settled on its dregs, friends. The verse says Moab has not gone into exile (Jeremiah 48:11).

The answer is pour him out and shatter his jars. The LORD says the wanderers "…will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars." The wine that sat still so long finally gets emptied. And the jars don't survive it, friends (Jeremiah 48:12).

The answer is Chemosh. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33). Back in verse 7, he's the one going into exile, friends (Jeremiah 48:13, 48:7).

The answer is False. The King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts, says the best of Moab's young men "…have gone down in the slaughter…" There's no victory in that verse, friends. It's a hard one to read (Jeremiah 48:15).

The answer is that it is at hand and rushing swiftly. The verse says, "Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly." No long wait on this one, friends. It's already close and coming fast (Jeremiah 48:16).

The answer is False. The LORD tells all who surround Moab, "Mourn for him…" and to tell how the mighty scepter is shattered. No celebrating is called for, friends. It's a call to grieve (Jeremiah 48:17).

The answer is that the destroyer of Moab has come against her. She's told to come down from her glory because "…the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses." Dibon is under attack, friends. She's told to sit on parched ground (Jeremiah 48:18).
The answer is shattered. The verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Shattered, like the jars in verse 12, friends. The picture holds together (Jeremiah 48:20, 48:12).

The answer is True. The LORD closes with, "The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken…" Both pictures are about Moab's strength being gone, friends. Then the verse ends with, "…declares the LORD…" (Jeremiah 48:25).
